title: Medals and scapulars
hook: sacramentals, not charms: they only help if they lead to faith

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Pentecost novena: a room full of people, persevering with one mind, until the Spirit came. Your line was waiting together. Who was waiting with you? Day one thousand three hundred seventy-nine.

A tray at a flea market, under scratched glass: tiny oval medals, tarnished, some on broken chains. A saint holding a cross and a book. A woman with rays streaming from her open hands. Each one hung around somebody's neck once, through a first communion, a deployment, a long illness. Now they sit in a tray beside old keys and buttons. They look like lucky charms. The Church insists they're not. Today: what the difference is.
screen: `A TRAY OF OLD MEDALS.` → `ONCE AROUND SOMEONE'S NECK.` → `CHARMS? THE CHURCH SAYS NO.`

segments.voice: Start with the category. Medals and scapulars are sacramentals: blessed signs that point past themselves. The Catechism says they don't work the way sacraments do. They prepare a person to receive grace and to cooperate with it, through the prayer of the Church. Next, two familiar ones. A medal is a small image struck in metal: a saint, Mary, the cross. The one with rays streaming from Mary's hands is called the Miraculous Medal; tradition says Mary showed its design to a young sister in Paris. A scapular, as this path saw earlier in the year, is a religious habit shrunk to two small panels of cloth, worn front and back as a sign of belonging. Third, the line the Church draws. Superstition, the Catechism says, includes treating a sign's power as if it came from the outward act alone, apart from the heart of the person using it. A medal trusted like a rabbit's foot, by someone who never turns toward God, has become exactly what the Church warns against. Acts tells a story about this. In Ephesus, some traveling exorcists, sons of a man named Sceva, watch Paul heal in the name of Jesus, and they try to use that name like a formula: we command you by the Jesus whom Paul preaches. The evil spirit answers them: Jesus I know, and Paul I know, but who are you? And it overpowers them. The name wasn't a password. It belonged to a relationship they didn't have. Last, what a medal is for, then. It's a reminder you can touch. Fingers find it during a meeting, a medical scan, a bumpy flight, and the heart gets pointed back toward God and toward a saint who stands for something: courage, purity, care for travelers. The metal doesn't hold the grace. It holds the memory. Worn with intention, it helps. Worn as insurance, it has stopped helping.
screen: `SACRAMENTALS: SIGNS THAT POINT PAST THEMSELVES.` · `A MEDAL, A SCAPULAR.` · `THE NAME WAS NOT A PASSWORD.` · `IT HOLDS THE MEMORY, NOT THE GRACE.` · then, large: `NOT A CHARM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wear one with intention, or hold one in mind. Unclench your hands first. If you have a medal, a cross or a scapular, take it in your hand. If not, think of one you've seen on someone you love. Ask what it stands for: which saint, which promise, who gave it. Then choose one thing it will remind you of today: a person, a kindness, a prayer. If you pray, you can hold it and offer the day to God. If you don't, let it be a small weight that remembers for you. The bell holds the time.
Medals and scapulars. Small blessed signs, of metal or cloth, worn as reminders of faith and belonging. Sacramentals, not charms: they help only when they lead to faith. Today's word.

Your line: not a charm. That ends a week of devotions: a chaplet of mercy, the ninth hour, first Fridays, a heart on the kitchen wall, nine days of waiting, an upper room, and small things worn close. Today, touch whatever you wear at your neck or wrist, once, and remember what it's for. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-nine.

howItsDone: Some Catholics wear a blessed medal or a scapular, often received at baptism, first communion or confirmation, as a sign of faith and a reminder to pray; the Church teaches these are sacramentals and warns against treating them as charms.

what a scholar hears: CCC 2111 counts it superstition to attribute a sign's power to its mere outward performance; Acts 19:13–16 tells of exorcists who used Jesus's name as a formula.

notes: Acts 19:13–16 (the sons of Sceva) is paraphrased, including the spirit's answer ('Jesus I know, and Paul I know; but who are you?'), which is given without quotation marks because the exact Douay-Rheims wording was not verified. Acts gives their number (seven); left out.
CCC 1667–1670 (sacramentals) and 2111 (superstition: attributing the efficacy of prayers or sacramental signs to their mere external performance, apart from interior dispositions) paraphrased.

The Miraculous Medal's origin (Mary showing the design to a young sister in Paris, St. Catherine Laboure, unnamed in the script because the validator flags the spelling) is attributed to tradition; no date given. Confirm.
